name: ProCoach
tagline: Coaching marketplace — Next.js, React, TypeScript, Tailwind, shadcn/ui
context: A coaching marketplace connecting coaches, learners and parents: session discovery, enrollment, scheduling and role-specific dashboards, with JWT/OTP authentication, role-based access control, and Stripe Embedded Checkout / Stripe Connect surfaces for payments.

questions.question: What problem does ProCoach solve, and what was your role on it?
questions.thirtySec: ProCoach is a coaching marketplace where coaches, learners and parents can discover sessions, enroll, schedule and manage everything from role-specific dashboards. I owned the frontend end to end — architecture, components, and integration with the backend services.
questions.ninetySec: ProCoach solves the problem of connecting coaches with learners — and parents, when the learner is a minor — in one place: browsing available sessions, enrolling, scheduling around timezones, and paying through the platform. There are three distinct roles, each with a different dashboard and permission set. I was responsible for the entire frontend: the Next.js App Router architecture, the component and design system built with Tailwind and shadcn/ui, wiring up JWT/OTP authentication and role-based UI, and integrating Stripe for payments. I worked directly with backend REST services rather than building them myself.
questions.deepDive: The core complexity in ProCoach isn't any single screen — it's that the same product surface (sessions, dashboards, scheduling) behaves differently per role, and payments/timezones add real edge cases. I structured the frontend around feature folders rather than one global app state, so the enrollment flow, the scheduling flow and the payment flow each owned their own local state and only reached into shared context for auth/role information. That kept each workflow understandable in isolation instead of one large tangled store.
questions.weak: A weak answer just says "I built a coaching platform" without naming the three roles, the payment integration, or being specific about what "owning the frontend" actually meant day to day.
followUps: Who were the other people working on this — was there a backend team, a designer?
How big was the codebase, roughly, in terms of major feature areas?
questions.honestyWarning: Only describe backend collaboration, not backend ownership — you built and integrated the frontend against REST services, you did not say you built those services.

questions.question: What did you personally own on ProCoach, versus what was owned by others?
questions.thirtySec: I owned the entire frontend: architecture, UI components, state management, auth integration and payment UI. I did not own the backend services or infrastructure — I integrated against REST APIs that existed as separate services.
questions.ninetySec: My ownership was the frontend layer end to end: setting up the Next.js App Router structure, building the design system with Tailwind and shadcn/ui, implementing JWT/OTP-based authentication and role-based UI for coach/learner/parent, wiring up session discovery/enrollment/scheduling screens, and integrating Stripe Embedded Checkout and Connect surfaces for payments. Backend services — the REST APIs I consumed, and whatever handled OTP delivery, payment webhooks, and data persistence — were separate concerns I integrated with but did not build.
questions.deepDive: Ownership boundaries mattered a lot here because payments and auth are exactly the areas where frontend and backend responsibilities get blurry in an interview answer if you're not careful. On the frontend side, I decided the state shape for each feature, how errors from the REST services were normalized and displayed, how payment confirmation/loading/failure/retry states were represented in the UI, and how role information from the JWT translated into what a user could see and do. What I did not do was implement OTP generation/verification logic, payment webhook handling, or any database/service-level RBAC enforcement — those lived in the backend, and I always treated the frontend role checks as UX convenience, not security.
questions.weak: A weak answer blurs the line and implies you built or fully controlled the payment backend or OTP service — don't claim that.
followUps: If the backend RBAC and the frontend RBAC disagreed, what would happen?
How did you find out the shape of the REST API you were integrating with — was there a contract/spec?
questions.honestyWarning: Never claim you owned or secured the backend payment/auth logic — you consumed and integrated with it.

questions.question: How was the ProCoach frontend architected, and how did you break it into components?
questions.thirtySec: It was a Next.js App Router app organized by feature — session discovery, enrollment, scheduling, dashboards — each with its own components, rather than one flat components folder. Shared UI primitives came from shadcn/ui, styled with Tailwind.
questions.ninetySec: I organized the app by feature rather than by technical layer: session discovery, enrollment, scheduling and each role's dashboard were their own feature areas, each owning its components, hooks and local state. Cross-cutting concerns — auth context, the design system, shared API utilities — lived in shared modules that features imported from, not the other way around. shadcn/ui gave me accessible, composable primitives (dialogs, dropdowns, form controls) that I customized with Tailwind rather than building every primitive from scratch.
questions.deepDive: The architectural bet was: keep features independent so a change to the scheduling flow can't accidentally break the payment flow. Layouts in the App Router mapped naturally to this — a role-specific layout (coach/learner/parent) wrapped its own set of pages, and shared layouts handled things like the top nav and auth guard. For component design, I leaned on composition over configuration — for example, a SessionCard component that accepted children/slots for role-specific actions, rather than a single component with a dozen boolean props controlling every variant.
questions.weak: A weak answer says "I used Next.js and components" without describing any actual boundary or organizing principle.
followUps: How did shared layouts differ between coach, learner and parent?
Did you use any component library conventions (like compound components) beyond shadcn/ui's defaults?

questions.question: How did you manage state across ProCoach's different dashboards and workflows?
questions.thirtySec: I deliberately kept state feature-local instead of putting everything in one global store — auth/role info lived in a small shared context, but enrollment, scheduling and payment state stayed inside their own workflows.
questions.ninetySec: Rather than reaching for one large global state container, I treated most state as belonging to the feature that created it. Enrollment flow state, scheduling flow state, and payment confirmation state each lived close to where they were used, often as component or feature-level state, with React Query-style data fetching (or an equivalent fetch-and-cache pattern) for anything that mirrored server data. The only truly global piece was authentication/role state, exposed through context, because almost every feature needed to read "who is logged in and what role are they" without prop drilling.
questions.deepDive: This was a conscious trade-off: a single global store is tempting because it feels organized, but it couples unrelated features together and makes it harder to reason about what changes when. By keeping feature state local, a bug in the scheduling flow's state couldn't leak into the payment flow's state, and I could reason about each workflow in isolation when debugging. Server state (session lists, enrollment status) was treated differently from UI state (which step of a wizard you're on, whether a modal is open) — conflating those two is a common mistake I specifically avoided.
questions.weak: A weak answer says "I used Context for everything" or "I used Redux" without explaining why, or without distinguishing server state from UI state.
followUps: Where exactly did you draw the line between "goes in context" and "stays local"?
How did you avoid prop drilling for role-based UI without over-using context?

questions.question: How did ProCoach integrate with backend REST services, and how did you handle errors?
questions.thirtySec: ProCoach talked to multiple REST services, so I built a consistent API layer that normalized responses and errors, and every screen had explicit loading, error and empty states rather than assuming the happy path.
questions.ninetySec: Because ProCoach depended on multiple REST services rather than one monolithic API, I put effort into a consistent integration layer: a shared request wrapper that attached auth headers, normalized error shapes coming from different services (which didn't always agree on error format), and gave every data-fetching hook a predictable loading/error/success/empty shape. That meant a component consuming session data didn't need to know which service it came from — it just handled the same four states every other component did.
questions.deepDive: The multiple-services part is the real interview-worthy detail: different backend services occasionally returned errors in different shapes, so I normalized them at the boundary into one consistent error object (message, code, field-level errors where relevant) before they ever reached a component. For payments specifically, error handling had to be more careful — a failed payment call needed a clear retry path without risking a duplicate charge, so mutations were not blindly auto-retried the way a GET request might be.
questions.weak: A weak answer says "I used try/catch" without describing normalization across multiple services or without distinguishing safe-to-retry reads from unsafe-to-retry writes.
followUps: How did the API layer handle a 401 partway through a session?
Did you use Axios interceptors, and what did they handle?

questions.question: What were the most complex workflows in ProCoach, and how did you handle failure cases in them?
questions.thirtySec: Enrollment and scheduling were the most complex, because they combine role permissions, timezone-sensitive session times, and payment status all in one flow — each step needed its own explicit failure and retry handling.
questions.ninetySec: The enrollment-to-payment flow was the most complex: a learner or parent finds a session, enrolls, and pays — and each of those steps could fail independently. Scheduling added timezone sensitivity on top, since coaches, learners and parents could be in different timezones and the session time had to be displayed correctly and unambiguously for everyone. I made sure each step in the flow had its own explicit state (not just one big "isLoading" flag for the whole page) so a payment failure didn't look like an enrollment failure, and the user always knew exactly what had and hadn't succeeded.
questions.deepDive: For timezones, the rule I followed was: store and reason about times in UTC, and only convert to the viewer's local timezone at the display boundary — never do timezone math in the middle of business logic. For the enrollment/payment flow, I modeled each stage as its own status (enrolling, awaiting-payment, payment-processing, confirmed, failed) rather than a single boolean, which made it possible to show the right retry action at the right stage instead of a generic "something went wrong" message.
questions.weak: A weak answer treats timezones as "just use the browser's timezone" without acknowledging DST or coach/learner timezone mismatches, or collapses a multi-step flow into one loading state.
followUps: How did you handle a session near a DST transition?
What did the UI show if payment succeeded but enrollment confirmation was delayed?

questions.question: What did you do for performance and testing on ProCoach?
questions.thirtySec: Since it was statically hosted with dynamic workflows layered on top, I paid attention to what could be pre-rendered versus what had to stay client-driven, and I tested the riskiest flows — auth and payment — most carefully.
questions.ninetySec: For performance, the static-hosting constraint meant being deliberate about which parts of a page could be static and which needed client-side data. I kept client-side JavaScript scoped to the interactive pieces (forms, payment widgets, role-aware navigation) rather than making entire pages client components. For testing, I focused effort where the risk was highest — authentication flows and payment status handling — rather than spreading thin, equal test coverage across every screen.
questions.deepDive: I'm being honest here rather than overselling: testing coverage wasn't exhaustive across the whole app. Given real time constraints, I prioritized the flows where a bug would be worst for the user — a payment showing the wrong status, or a role seeing content it shouldn't. Performance-wise, the biggest lever was avoiding unnecessary client-side JavaScript given the static-hosting model, and being careful with image and font loading since those affect perceived load time the most on a marketing-adjacent, discovery-heavy product.
questions.weak: A weak answer claims comprehensive automated test coverage or specific performance numbers that were never actually measured.
followUps: What testing tools did you use, if any?
What would you test first if you had one more week?
questions.honestyWarning: Do not claim specific performance metrics (load time improvements, Lighthouse scores) or test coverage percentages that were never measured — describe the approach and priorities honestly instead.

questions.question: What trade-offs did you make on ProCoach, what would you improve today, and how did you collaborate with backend and other stakeholders?
questions.thirtySec: The biggest trade-off was static hosting for speed and simplicity versus the extra care needed for dynamic, role-based and payment workflows. Today I'd push earlier for a documented API contract with the backend to avoid integration surprises. I worked directly with backend developers to align on request/response shapes.
questions.ninetySec: Static hosting with dynamic workflows layered on top was a deliberate trade-off — it kept hosting simple and fast for the discovery-heavy parts of the product, at the cost of extra care needed for anything dynamic or role-specific, which had to be handled carefully client-side or via revalidation. Working with backend developers meant regularly clarifying the exact shape of REST responses, especially for payment status and role/permission data, since assumptions there directly caused frontend bugs. If I rebuilt it today, I'd push for an agreed API contract (even a lightweight OpenAPI/TypeScript-types-shared approach) earlier, rather than discovering shape mismatches during integration.
questions.deepDive: The honest retrospective: static export is a great fit until a feature needs something dynamic that the export model fights against — and payment/timezone-sensitive scheduling are exactly those features. I'd likely reconsider a mixed rendering strategy (dynamic where it's truly needed, static everywhere else) rather than defaulting to static-first, now that I've seen where the friction actually showed up. On collaboration, the useful pattern was treating the backend team's API as a real interface — flagging shape changes early, and pushing back when an error response was inconsistent with other endpoints — rather than silently working around it in the frontend.
questions.weak: A weak answer either has no real trade-off to name, or claims to have made backend/infrastructure decisions that weren't actually the frontend's to make.
followUps: Did you ever have to push back on an API design decision? What happened?
If you had a dedicated backend teammate from day one, what would you have asked them to change?
questions.honestyWarning: Frame collaboration as influence and clarification, not as making backend architecture decisions yourself.

questions.question: Why Next.js for ProCoach?
questions.thirtySec: Next.js gave file-based routing, layouts for the different roles, and a path to mix static and dynamic rendering as needed — useful for a marketplace with discovery pages and role-specific dashboards.
questions.ninetySec: ProCoach needed both content-heavy, discovery-style pages (browsing coaches and sessions) and more dynamic, authenticated dashboard experiences for three different roles. Next.js let me use layouts to share structure per role, handle routing without hand-rolling a router, and choose rendering strategy per route instead of committing the whole app to one model. It also came with sensible defaults for image/font optimization, which mattered for the discovery pages.
questions.deepDive: The alternative would have been a plain React SPA with React Router — that works, but I'd have had to build layout nesting, route-based code splitting and any SSR/SSG capability by hand. Next.js's conventions removed that overhead and matched the shape of the product naturally: shared role layouts, nested routes for sub-flows like scheduling, and the option to statically render marketing/discovery pages while keeping authenticated areas dynamic.
questions.weak: A weak answer just says "Next.js is popular" or "it's what I know" without connecting it to ProCoach's actual routing/role/rendering needs.
followUps: What would you have lost by using a plain React SPA instead?
Did you use any Next.js-specific optimization features directly (next/image, next/font)?

questions.question: Why the App Router specifically, rather than the Pages Router?
questions.thirtySec: The App Router's nested layouts mapped directly onto ProCoach's role-based structure — a shared layout per role with nested pages underneath — and Server/Client Component separation let me keep more of the app server-rendered by default.
questions.ninetySec: The App Router's layout nesting was the deciding factor: coach, learner and parent each needed their own persistent navigation/shell, with pages nested underneath that shouldn't re-render the shared layout on every navigation. The Pages Router doesn't give you that natively. The App Router's Server/Client Component model also let me default to server-rendered where possible and only mark the truly interactive leaves (forms, payment widgets) as client components, which the Pages Router's all-client model doesn't offer.
questions.deepDive: Beyond layouts, the App Router's per-segment loading.tsx/error.tsx meant I could show a loading state for just the dashboard content while the shared shell stayed mounted, instead of a full-page spinner. That's a meaningfully better UX for a dashboard-heavy product where the user is switching between sections often.
questions.weak: A weak answer treats "App Router" and "Pages Router" as interchangeable, or can't explain what nested layouts actually buy you.
followUps: Did you hit any App Router rough edges (e.g. around caching or client boundaries) that you had to work around?

questions.question: Why keep feature-level state close to the workflow instead of a large global store?
questions.thirtySec: Because enrollment, scheduling and payment are largely independent workflows — coupling their state through one global store would make each harder to reason about and easier to break by accident.
questions.ninetySec: A global store optimizes for state that many unrelated parts of the app need at once. Most of ProCoach's state wasn't like that — it belonged to one workflow at a time. Keeping it feature-local meant I could open the enrollment flow's code and understand its entire state without checking what else in the app might be reading or writing to a shared store. The only state that genuinely was cross-cutting — auth/role — went into a small shared context instead.
questions.deepDive: This also paid off for change isolation: when the payment flow needed a new status value, that change stayed inside the payment feature's state and types, and nothing else in the app needed to know or care. A global store tends to invite exactly the kind of unrelated coupling that makes a change in one screen risk breaking another — and for a solo/small-team frontend, keeping that blast radius small mattered more than the theoretical convenience of one store.
questions.weak: A weak answer says "global state is bad" as a blanket rule without explaining the actual coupling risk it avoids, or without acknowledging that some cross-cutting state (auth) still needed to be shared.
followUps: What would have pushed you toward a global store instead?
How did shared auth/role context avoid becoming a dumping ground for other state over time?

questions.question: How did the coach/learner/parent RBAC work?
questions.thirtySec: The JWT carried role information, which drove both route-level access (which layouts/pages a role could reach) and UI-level rendering (which actions/sections were shown) — but the backend enforced permissions independently, since the frontend check is only UX.
questions.ninetySec: After JWT/OTP authentication, the token's role claim determined which role-specific layout and navigation the user saw, and components used that role to conditionally render actions — for example, only coaches could see session-management controls, only parents could see a linked learner's enrollment history. Route access was gated so a learner couldn't simply navigate to a coach-only URL and see coach-only data render. But I was always explicit, including in code review discussions, that this was a UX convenience — the backend independently enforced permission checks on every request, because a determined user can bypass any frontend-only gate.
questions.deepDive: The three-role model added a wrinkle beyond simple two-role RBAC: parents needed visibility into a linked learner's activity without having the learner's own permissions — a "delegated, read-mostly" access pattern rather than a strict role hierarchy. I modeled permissions as a small set of capability checks (canEnroll, canManageSessions, canViewLinkedLearner) derived from role plus relationship data, rather than hardcoding "if role === coach" checks scattered across components, which made the permission logic easier to audit in one place.
questions.weak: A weak answer implies the frontend RBAC is the actual security boundary, or can't explain how the parent role differed from a simple hierarchy.
followUps: How would you audit all the places a role check happens, to make sure none were missed?
What happens in the UI if a JWT expires mid-session?
questions.honestyWarning: Always state plainly that backend authorization enforcement is independent of and more important than any frontend role check.

questions.question: How was Stripe Embedded Checkout integrated?
questions.thirtySec: Stripe Embedded Checkout was mounted inside the enrollment flow so payment happened without a full redirect away from the product, and the frontend reacted to the checkout session's status rather than handling raw card data itself.
questions.ninetySec: I integrated Stripe's Embedded Checkout component into the enrollment flow so the payment UI lived inside ProCoach's own page rather than redirecting to a separate Stripe-hosted page. The frontend never touched raw card details — Stripe's embedded element handled that — and instead the frontend's job was creating a checkout session (via the backend), rendering the embedded element, and then reacting to the resulting status (success, failure, requires action) to move the enrollment flow forward or show a retry.
questions.deepDive: The key architectural point is that all sensitive payment operations and secret keys stayed server-side — the frontend only ever used Stripe's publishable key and the client-side embedded component, never a secret key. For Stripe Connect surfaces specifically, the frontend rendered coach-facing onboarding/status UI, but again the sensitive account-linking operations were backend-driven; the frontend's role was presenting status and guiding the coach through whatever step came next.
questions.weak: A weak answer suggests the frontend directly processed card numbers or held a Stripe secret key — both would be a real security red flag in an interview.
followUps: Where does the Stripe secret key live, and why must it never reach the browser?
What did the Stripe Connect onboarding status UI look like for a coach mid-onboarding?
questions.honestyWarning: Never suggest that any Stripe secret key or raw card data was handled in frontend code — Embedded Checkout is specifically designed so the frontend never touches either.

questions.question: How were payment success, failure and retry states handled?
questions.thirtySec: Each payment attempt had its own explicit status — pending, processing, succeeded, failed — displayed clearly, with a retry path for failures that didn't risk double-charging or double-booking the session.
questions.ninetySec: I modeled payment state as its own explicit status rather than a boolean, because "loading" isn't the same as "Stripe is processing" isn't the same as "webhook confirmation pending." The UI reflected each of those distinctly, so a user waiting on webhook confirmation saw a clear "confirming your payment" state rather than either a stuck spinner or a false success message. On failure, the retry path re-initiated a new checkout session rather than blindly resubmitting the same one, to avoid ambiguous double-submission states.
questions.deepDive: One subtlety worth mentioning: because Stripe payment confirmation can involve a webhook arriving asynchronously relative to the client-side redirect/response, the frontend couldn't always assume "checkout returned success" meant "enrollment is fully confirmed." I treated the client-side result as provisional and the source of truth as whatever the backend considered confirmed (informed by the webhook), polling or re-fetching enrollment status briefly if needed rather than assuming the client-side result was final.
questions.weak: A weak answer assumes the client-side checkout result is always immediately authoritative and ignores the async nature of webhook-driven confirmation.
followUps: What did the UI show during the gap between checkout redirect and webhook confirmation?
How did you avoid a user paying twice by clicking retry too fast?

questions.question: How did having multiple API services affect the frontend architecture?
questions.thirtySec: I built a normalization layer so components never had to know which service a piece of data came from — consistent request/response/error shapes regardless of the underlying service.
questions.ninetySec: Multiple REST services meant inconsistent conventions were a real risk — different pagination shapes, different error formats, maybe different auth header expectations. I handled this by putting a thin API layer between the raw services and the rest of the app: each service got its own client module, but they all exposed the same normalized shape (data, error, loading) to the features that consumed them. That meant a feature like the dashboard, which might combine data from two services, didn't have to special-case each one.
questions.deepDive: This also mattered for resilience: if one service was slower or occasionally flaky, I could isolate that in its client module (timeouts, retries for safe GET requests) without that logic leaking into every component that happened to use that service. It also made it easier to reason about caching and revalidation per service, since they didn't necessarily share the same freshness requirements — session availability data needed to feel near-real-time, while a coach's profile data could tolerate more staleness.
questions.weak: A weak answer treats "multiple services" as a trivial detail rather than something that actively shaped the API layer's design.
followUps: Did any two services ever disagree about the same piece of data? How did you resolve that?

questions.question: How were timezone issues handled for sessions?
questions.thirtySec: Session times were stored and reasoned about in UTC everywhere in business logic, and converted to each viewer's local timezone only at the point of display.
questions.ninetySec: Because coaches, learners and parents could be in different timezones, I made sure every session time was stored and compared in UTC internally, and only converted to a human-readable, viewer-local time at the UI layer — never in the middle of scheduling logic. This avoided a whole class of bugs where a session looked like it was at a different time to different roles, or where date-only comparisons silently broke across a timezone boundary.
questions.deepDive: The trickiest part is daylight saving time transitions and displaying a time in a way that's unambiguous — I made sure the UI always showed the timezone abbreviation or offset alongside the time, rather than a bare "3:00 PM" that's ambiguous the moment two people are in different zones. Any date-only logic (like "is this session today") was computed against the viewer's local calendar day, not the UTC calendar day, since those can disagree near midnight.
questions.weak: A weak answer says "we used the browser's timezone" without addressing DST, without showing the offset/timezone in the UI, or without separating storage (UTC) from display (local).
followUps: How would you test a session scheduled right across a DST transition?
What would you show if a coach and learner were about to have a session but their local "now" showed different dates?

questions.question: What were the limitations of static export for ProCoach?
questions.thirtySec: Static export meant no server-side logic at request time, so anything requiring per-request dynamic data or secrets had to be handled client-side or via separate API calls, which added complexity for authenticated, role-specific and payment-related pages.
questions.ninetySec: Static export pre-renders pages at build time, which is great for discovery/marketing-style content but doesn't fit pages whose content depends on the logged-in user's role or real-time data. For ProCoach, that meant authenticated dashboards, role-specific views and payment status pages had to fetch their dynamic content client-side after the static shell loaded, rather than having it baked in or server-rendered per request. That's a real trade-off: faster/cheaper hosting, but more client-side data-fetching complexity and a brief "shell then content" loading state on every dynamic page.
questions.deepDive: It also constrained anything that would normally live in a Next.js server context — middleware-based redirects for auth, or server-only secrets used per request — since static export doesn't run a server at request time. Anything security-sensitive had to be enforced by the backend regardless, and the frontend's job became gracefully handling "not yet authenticated" or "wrong role" states client-side after the static page had already loaded, rather than preventing that content from ever being sent.
questions.weak: A weak answer doesn't know what static export actually gives up (no per-request server logic) and treats it as just "a faster version of SSR".
followUps: If ProCoach dropped static export tomorrow, what would you change first?
How did you avoid a flash of "wrong role" content before the client-side auth check resolved?

questions.question: How would the architecture change at larger scale?
questions.thirtySec: I'd reconsider static export in favor of a mixed rendering strategy, introduce a shared, documented API contract with the backend, and likely extract the design system and API client layer into their own packages if multiple products started sharing them.
questions.ninetySec: At larger scale, the static-export trade-off would likely stop paying for itself — I'd move authenticated and role-specific routes to dynamic rendering while keeping discovery/marketing pages static, using the App Router's per-route flexibility rather than an all-or-nothing choice. I'd also want a shared, typed contract between frontend and backend (generated types from an API schema) to remove the "discovering the shape by testing it" friction I mentioned earlier. If the multiple REST services grew further, I'd consider a thin BFF (backend-for-frontend) layer to aggregate and normalize them server-side instead of doing it entirely in the browser.
questions.deepDive: I'd be careful here not to overengineer preemptively — a BFF, a monorepo design system package, and a shared schema registry are all real costs (more infrastructure, more indirection) that only pay off once the pain they solve is actually being felt (e.g. multiple frontends needing the same normalized data, or type drift causing repeated bugs). The honest answer is: scale the architecture in response to concrete pain points you've actually hit, not in anticipation of hypothetical future ones.
questions.weak: A weak answer lists impressive-sounding infrastructure (microservices, GraphQL federation, a monorepo) without connecting each choice to a specific problem it would solve.
followUps: What's the first concrete sign that static export was no longer the right choice?
How would you introduce a BFF without a big-bang rewrite?

name: KhetiValah
tagline: Agriculture marketplace & event booking — React, TypeScript, Tailwind, Spring Boot REST APIs
context: An agriculture marketplace and event-booking platform for vendors, sponsors, farmers, buyers and participants: product listings, stall booking, participant registration, Razorpay payments, GST billing/invoicing, OTP authentication and role-based routing.
stack: Spring Boot REST APIs (backend, consumed not built)

questions.question: What problem does KhetiValah solve, and what was your role?
questions.thirtySec: KhetiValah is an agriculture marketplace and event-booking platform serving vendors, sponsors, farmers, buyers and participants — product listings, stall booking and event registration in one place. I built the frontend in React/TypeScript/Tailwind, integrating against Spring Boot REST APIs built by the backend team.
questions.ninetySec: KhetiValah brings together several distinct user types around agriculture commerce and events: vendors and sponsors listing products or sponsoring stalls, farmers and buyers trading, and participants registering for events. That range of roles meant a lot of role-based routing and permission logic. I owned the React/TypeScript frontend — catalog and listing UIs, stall booking and participant registration flows, Razorpay payment integration, GST billing/invoice interfaces, and OTP-based authentication — while the Spring Boot REST APIs were built and owned by the backend team.
questions.deepDive: The interesting complexity here is the breadth of roles compared to ProCoach's three — vendors, sponsors, farmers, buyers and participants each needed a somewhat different subset of the product surface, so role-based routing had to scale to more than a simple two-or-three-way branch. I approached it as a capability-based system (what can this role do) rather than hardcoding per-role page trees everywhere, which kept the routing logic maintainable as more role combinations came up.
questions.weak: A weak answer treats all these roles as interchangeable "users" without acknowledging how differently vendors, sponsors, farmers, buyers and participants actually use the product.
followUps: Could a single person hold more than one role, e.g. both a farmer and a buyer?
How did you decide what counted as a distinct role versus a permission flag?
questions.honestyWarning: The backend (Spring Boot APIs) was built by the backend team — describe your role as frontend integration and collaboration, not backend ownership.

questions.question: What did you personally own on KhetiValah?
questions.thirtySec: I owned the React/TypeScript frontend: catalog and listings, stall booking, participant registration, Razorpay checkout UI, GST billing/invoice screens, OTP auth flows and role-based routing — all integrated against Spring Boot REST APIs I did not build.
questions.ninetySec: My ownership covered the whole frontend surface: product/catalog listings, the stall booking and participant registration flows, the Razorpay payment UI and its confirmation/failure states, GST billing and invoice display, OTP-based login, and the role-based routing that determined what each user type could reach. The Spring Boot backend — the actual API implementations, database, and business rule enforcement — was owned by backend engineers; my job was consuming those APIs correctly and handling every state they could return.
questions.deepDive: Because GST billing and payments were involved, I was careful to keep the frontend's responsibility scoped to correctly displaying and collecting the data the backend needed (e.g. GST-relevant fields on a registration or purchase form) and correctly rendering whatever billing/invoice data the backend returned — not computing GST logic itself, which is a backend/compliance concern.

questions.question: Why WebSockets for RDR Tech?
questions.thirtySec: Because audit/approval workflows needed near-real-time visibility across users — polling would either be too slow to feel current or too frequent to be efficient, so a persistent WebSocket connection made more sense.
questions.ninetySec: The workflow nature of the product — tasks moving through approval stages that multiple people care about simultaneously — meant staleness was a real usability problem: someone approving a task while looking at outdated status information is a genuine risk in an audit context. Polling on a short interval could approximate real time but wastes requests and still has a visible lag; WebSockets let the server push updates the moment something changed, which fit the operational, time-sensitive nature of audit workflows much better.
questions.deepDive: I was also mindful not to over-apply WebSockets everywhere — parts of the app that didn't need real-time freshness (e.g. static reference data) still used regular REST calls. The WebSocket connection was reserved for the genuinely time-sensitive slice of the product: task/approval status changes and any live document activity.

questions.question: How did you handle WebSocket reconnection?
questions.thirtySec: The client tracked connection state explicitly (connected/reconnecting/disconnected), retried with backoff on drop, and re-synced state after reconnecting rather than assuming nothing had changed while disconnected.
questions.ninetySec: I modeled the WebSocket connection's status as its own piece of UI state, shown to the user (so they'd know if they were looking at potentially stale data), and implemented reconnection with exponential backoff rather than immediate rapid retries that could hammer the server. On successful reconnection, the client didn't just resume listening for new events — it also re-fetched or reconciled current state, since events that occurred while disconnected would otherwise be silently missed.
questions.deepDive: The reconnection-plus-resync pattern was the important part: a naive reconnect that just re-opens the socket and waits for the next event leaves a gap for anything that happened during the disconnected window. I treated "just reconnected" as a trigger to re-sync a snapshot of relevant state, then resume applying incremental events from that point.

questions.question: What happens when duplicate or out-of-order events arrive?

questions.ninetySec: I couldn't assume WebSocket events would always arrive exactly once and in order — network conditions and reconnects make that unsafe to assume. Each event carried enough information (an id, and ideally a version or timestamp) to let the client detect "I've already applied this" and skip it, making event application idempotent. For ordering, where an event included a version/sequence number for the entity it affected, I applied it only if it represented a newer state than what was already held locally, rather than blindly overwriting with whatever arrived last in wall-clock time.

Without this, a slightly delayed "task moved to draft" event arriving after a newer "task approved" event could incorrectly roll back the UI's view of the task's status.

followUps: Did the frontend and backend ever disagree about a valid transition? How was that caught?

questions.question: How did you organize dense dashboard data specifically, beyond just "widgets"?
questions.thirtySec: Each widget owned its own data-fetching/WebSocket-subscription lifecycle and loading/error/empty state, so failures or slow data in one widget never blocked or broke the rest of the dashboard.
questions.ninetySec: Beyond just splitting into widgets visually, each widget managed its own async lifecycle independently — its own loading spinner, its own error-with-retry state, and, where relevant, its own subscription to the subset of WebSocket events it cared about. That isolation meant a slow or failing "recent document activity" widget didn't block the "tasks by status" chart from rendering, which matters a lot on a dashboard many people rely on throughout the day.
questions.deepDive: I also thought about update frequency per widget — not every widget needed to react to every event type, so widgets subscribed only to the event types relevant to them, reducing unnecessary re-renders across the dashboard when an unrelated event arrived.
questions.weak: A weak answer has one shared loading/error state for the whole dashboard, meaning one failure blanks out everything.
followUps: How did you decide which WebSocket event types each widget should subscribe to?

questions.question: How would you test real-time behaviour in RDR Tech?
questions.thirtySec: With a mock WebSocket server/client that can script scenarios — disconnect mid-session, deliver duplicate events, deliver events out of order — since these are the failure modes that matter most and are hardest to trigger manually.
questions.ninetySec: Testing real-time behavior manually against a live connection can't reliably reproduce timing-dependent bugs, so the right approach is a mock WebSocket layer that lets tests script exact scenarios: send event A then a duplicate of A, or send an older-versioned event after a newer one, or simulate a disconnect mid-flow and verify the resync logic correctly reconciles state afterward. Each of the reconciliation rules described earlier (idempotency, version-based ordering, resync-after-reconnect) is specifically testable this way, because the mock gives full control over delivery order and timing that a real socket wouldn't.
questions.deepDive: Being honest, building this kind of mock harness is itself real engineering work that's easy to underinvest in under deadline pressure — which is exactly why I'd flag it as the top improvement area rather than claim it was already fully built out.
questions.weak: A weak answer says "we'd write unit tests" without describing what's actually hard to test here (timing, ordering, duplication) or how a mock would address it.
followUps: What's the minimum mock WebSocket harness you'd build first, given limited time?

name: SGreens ERP
context: An ERP system for poultry production, inventory, purchases, sales, hatchery and accounts: reactive forms, large tables with pagination/filtering/search, JWT-aware REST integration, and role-based operational interfaces.

questions.question: What problem does SGreens ERP solve, and what was your role?
questions.thirtySec: SGreens ERP covers poultry production, inventory, purchases, sales, hatchery and accounts for the business — an operational system built with Angular, TypeScript and PrimeNG. I built the frontend: reactive forms, large tables, and role-based modules.
questions.ninetySec: SGreens ERP is an operational system covering the full poultry business — production, inventory, purchases, sales, hatchery operations and accounts — each a distinct module with its own forms and tables. I owned the Angular frontend: building reactive forms for data entry across these modules, large PrimeNG-based tables with pagination/filtering/search, and JWT-aware integration with REST APIs, all gated by role-based access per module.
questions.deepDive: What made this project distinct from the others is the sheer number of operational modules (production, inventory, purchases, sales, hatchery, accounts) each with their own tables and forms — the real engineering challenge was consistency and reuse across modules rather than any single complex workflow. A poorly reused table or form pattern here would multiply maintenance cost across six-plus modules instead of just one.
questions.weak: A weak answer describes it as "a CRUD app" without acknowledging the operational breadth (six-plus distinct business modules) that's the actual complexity driver.
followUps: Which module had the most complex data relationships?

questions.question: What did you personally own on SGreens ERP?
questions.thirtySec: I owned the Angular frontend across all modules: reactive forms, PrimeNG tables with pagination/filtering/search, JWT-aware API integration, and role-based module access.
questions.ninetySec: My ownership spanned the frontend for production, inventory, purchases, sales, hatchery and accounts modules — building consistent reactive forms and PrimeNG data tables across all of them, wiring up JWT-aware REST integration (attaching tokens, handling expiry), and implementing role-based access so different operational roles saw only their relevant modules. The backend APIs and business logic (like actual inventory calculations or accounting rules) were separate concerns I integrated with.
questions.deepDive: A specific piece of ownership worth naming: I built shared, reusable patterns (a common table component configuration, shared form validation patterns) precisely because six-plus modules with entirely separate, one-off implementations would have been a maintenance burden — that reuse decision was itself part of the frontend architecture work, not just "building six separate features".
questions.weak: A weak answer implies you built the actual inventory/accounting business logic rather than just the UI/integration layer for it.
followUps: What was actually shared/reused across modules, concretely?
questions.honestyWarning: Frame inventory/accounting calculations as backend-owned business logic that the frontend displays and collects input for, not something the frontend computed.

questions.question: How were large tables designed across SGreens ERP's modules?
questions.thirtySec: A shared, configurable table pattern built on PrimeNG — column definitions, server-side pagination, filtering and search passed as configuration — reused across modules instead of one-off tables per module.
questions.ninetySec: Rather than building a bespoke table per module, I built toward a shared table configuration pattern on top of PrimeNG's table component: each module supplied its column definitions, which fields were filterable/sortable, and how pagination should behave, while the underlying table behavior (rendering, selection, responsive handling) stayed consistent. This meant a fix or improvement to table behavior (like a better empty state or a performance tweak) benefited every module at once instead of needing to be repeated six-plus times.
questions.deepDive: Given the data volumes typical of ERP systems (inventory records, transaction history), pagination was generally server-side rather than client-side — fetching and rendering an entire large dataset client-side isn't practical at ERP scale, so filtering and sorting parameters were sent to the backend and the table rendered whatever page it returned.
questions.weak: A weak answer describes each module's table as built independently from scratch, missing the reuse/consistency angle that matters at this scale.
followUps: How did you decide which modules could tolerate client-side pagination versus needing server-side?

questions.question: Client-side versus server-side pagination — how did you decide, in general?
questions.thirtySec: For any module with genuinely large or growing datasets (inventory, transaction history), server-side pagination; for small, bounded reference lists, client-side was acceptable and simpler.
questions.ninetySec: The deciding factor was realistic data volume and growth: inventory and transactional data in an ERP can grow into the thousands or more records, where fetching everything client-side would be slow and wasteful — so those used server-side pagination, filtering and sorting, with the backend doing the heavy lifting. For smaller, more bounded lists — reference data that doesn't grow much — client-side pagination was simpler to implement and perfectly adequate, and I didn't force server-side complexity where it wasn't needed.
questions.deepDive: This is a good example of avoiding both extremes: defaulting everything to server-side pagination adds unnecessary complexity to small reference-data screens, while defaulting everything to client-side would break down badly on the genuinely large modules. The decision was made per-module based on actual expected data volume, not a blanket rule.
questions.weak: A weak answer picks one approach for the entire ERP without considering that different modules have very different data volume profiles.
followUps: How would a module's pagination strategy need to change if its data volume grew 10x?

questions.question: How were repeated forms and tables reused across SGreens ERP?
questions.thirtySec: Shared reactive form building blocks (common validators, reusable field groups) and a shared table configuration pattern meant each module composed from common pieces instead of duplicating form/table code six-plus times.
questions.ninetySec: I extracted the parts of forms and tables that repeated across modules — common validators (required fields, numeric ranges, date constraints), reusable field-group components (like an address block or a quantity/unit-of-measure pair), and the shared table configuration pattern already described — so each module's form or table was mostly configuration plus whatever was genuinely unique to that module, rather than a full rebuild.
questions.deepDive: The trade-off I was careful about was not over-abstracting: some fields looked similar across modules but had subtly different validation rules (a hatchery quantity field versus a sales quantity field, for instance), so I kept the shared pieces focused on things that were genuinely identical, and let module-specific logic stay in the module rather than adding configuration flags to a shared component for every small difference.
questions.weak: A weak answer either has no reuse (six separate implementations) or over-abstracts into one form component with dozens of configuration flags trying to cover every module's edge case.
followUps: Give an example of two fields that looked similar across modules but you deliberately did NOT share.

questions.question: How was inventory consistency presented in the UI?
questions.thirtySec: Inventory figures were always displayed as backend-computed, authoritative values — the frontend didn't locally compute or cache stock levels across screens in a way that could drift from the source of truth.
questions.ninetySec: Given that inventory levels are affected by multiple modules (purchases increasing stock, sales decreasing it, production/hatchery affecting raw and finished stock), I made sure the frontend always treated the backend as the single source of truth for current inventory figures, re-fetching relevant data after any action that could change stock levels rather than optimistically adjusting a locally cached count that could silently drift from reality.
questions.deepDive: This is a case where optimistic UI updates — which I used elsewhere for less consequential state — were deliberately avoided, because showing an incorrect inventory figure, even briefly, in an operational ERP context is a worse outcome than a slightly slower, always-accurate refresh after a mutating action.
questions.weak: A weak answer applies the same optimistic-update pattern everywhere without recognizing that inventory correctness has a higher cost of being wrong than most other UI state.
followUps: Were there any inventory-related screens where you did use optimistic updates, and why was that safe there but not elsewhere?

questions.question: How did JWT-aware API integration work, and how were role-based modules controlled?
questions.thirtySec: A shared HTTP interceptor attached the JWT to requests and handled expiry/redirect-to-login centrally, and each operational role saw only the modules/actions their role granted, enforced independently by the backend as well.
questions.ninetySec: Angular's HTTP interceptor pattern was a natural fit for JWT handling — one interceptor attached the token to outgoing requests and handled a 401 (typically redirecting to login or attempting a refresh) centrally, so individual modules didn't need to repeat that logic. Role-based module access followed the same principle as the other projects: role determined which modules and actions appeared in the UI, but the backend independently enforced what each role could actually do — a purchasing-role user seeing only purchases and inventory modules was a UX convenience, not the actual security boundary.
questions.deepDive: Given the number of modules, I modeled role-to-module access as configuration data rather than scattering per-module role checks — a small map of role → allowed modules/actions that drove both navigation and route guards consistently.
questions.weak: A weak answer repeats JWT-attachment logic in every module's API calls instead of centralizing it in an interceptor, or implies frontend role gating is sufficient security.
followUps: What did the interceptor do on a 401 specifically — silent refresh, or redirect to login?
questions.honestyWarning: State clearly that backend enforcement of role-based permissions is independent of and required alongside frontend module gating.

questions.question: How would you modernize the Angular SGreens ERP frontend today?
questions.thirtySec: I'd evaluate a gradual move toward more modern Angular patterns (standalone components, signals) rather than a full rewrite, and I'd consider whether a React/Next.js rewrite is justified given my current stack depth — but only if the business case for a rewrite is real, not just for its own sake.
questions.ninetySec: A full rewrite is rarely the right first answer for a working ERP system that the business depends on daily — rewrites carry real risk and cost. I'd first look at modernizing incrementally within Angular: adopting newer patterns like standalone components and signals for more granular reactivity, tightening up the shared table/form abstractions based on what I've since learned works well, and improving type safety at the API boundary. A move to React/Next.js would only make sense if there were a concrete business driver — e.g. needing to share code/components with other products already built in React — not simply because it's the stack I now use more.
questions.deepDive: This question is really testing whether a candidate defaults to "rewrite it in my preferred stack" reflexively, which is a red flag. The honest, senior answer is: assess the actual pain points in the current system first (are there real bugs, real performance issues, real developer-velocity problems), and only propose the level of change that pain actually justifies — incremental modernization is usually the right call for a stable, working ERP.
questions.weak: A weak answer jumps straight to "rewrite it in React" without justifying why the rewrite cost would be worth it for a working system.
followUps: What would make a full rewrite actually justified here?

questions.question: How were large tables designed, in more technical detail?
questions.thirtySec: A shared PrimeNG-based table wrapper accepted column definitions and server-side pagination/filter/sort parameters as configuration, keeping rendering and interaction behavior consistent across all six-plus modules.
questions.ninetySec: The wrapper component took a typed column definition array (field, header, sortable, filterType) and emitted pagination/sort/filter change events that the parent module translated into API query parameters, then passed the returned page of data and total count back down. This kept the table's internal behavior (rendering rows, handling column sort UI, pagination controls) identical everywhere, while each module retained full control over what its API call actually did with those parameters.
questions.deepDive: For very large modules, I also considered virtualization for smoother scrolling on big pages, though the primary defense against large-data performance problems was server-side pagination itself — keeping the actually-rendered row count bounded per page rather than relying on virtualization to handle an unbounded dataset.
questions.weak: A weak answer has each module's table independently handling pagination/sort/filter logic with no shared contract.
followUps: What did the column definition type look like?

questions.question: Client-side versus server-side pagination — walk through a concrete example from SGreens ERP.
questions.thirtySec: Inventory transaction history used server-side pagination given its growing volume; a reference table like unit-of-measure types used client-side pagination since it was small and static.
questions.ninetySec: Inventory transaction history is a good concrete example: it grows continuously as purchases, sales and production events occur, so fetching the entire history client-side would become slower and slower over time — server-side pagination, filtering by date range, and search by reference number were essential there. By contrast, something like a unit-of-measure or category reference list was small, changed rarely, and was more responsive to filter client-side instantly without a network round-trip per keystroke — so client-side pagination and filtering made more sense there.
questions.deepDive: The general principle: pick pagination strategy based on the data's actual growth trajectory and interaction needs, not as a blanket architectural decision applied everywhere — this is the kind of trade-off discussion senior interviewers want to hear reasoned through with a real example, not just a rule stated abstractly.
questions.weak: A weak answer can't give a concrete example from the actual system and stays entirely abstract.
followUps: How would you migrate a module from client-side to server-side pagination if its data grew unexpectedly?

questions.question: How were repeated forms and tables reused, with a concrete example?
questions.thirtySec: A shared quantity/unit-of-measure field group was reused across purchases, sales and inventory forms, each supplying its own validation range while sharing the same layout and accessibility behavior.
questions.ninetySec: A concrete example: several modules needed a "quantity + unit of measure" input pair — purchases, sales and inventory adjustments all used it, but each had different valid ranges and sometimes different unit options. I built it as one reusable field-group component that accepted validation rules and allowed units as configuration, so the layout, accessibility labeling and basic interaction behavior stayed consistent everywhere, while each module supplied what made its usage specific.
questions.deepDive: This is the right granularity for reuse — reusing the presentation and interaction pattern while letting business rules vary per usage, rather than either duplicating the whole field three times or trying to hardcode one "true" set of validation rules into a shared component that wouldn't fit every module.
questions.weak: A weak answer either has no concrete reused example or describes over-abstracted shared components trying to cover every module's exact business rule.
followUps: How did each module supply its own validation rules to the shared component?

questions.question: How was inventory consistency presented, with a concrete failure mode you avoided?
questions.thirtySec: By always re-fetching authoritative stock levels after any mutating action (a purchase, a sale) rather than locally decrementing/incrementing a cached count, avoiding a scenario where two near-simultaneous actions leave the displayed count wrong.
questions.ninetySec: A concrete failure mode to avoid: if the UI optimistically decremented a local stock count on a sale before the backend confirmed it, and a purchase from another screen or user happened around the same time, the locally adjusted number could drift from the real, backend-computed value. Instead, after any action that could affect inventory, I re-fetched the authoritative figure from the backend rather than computing the new value client-side, accepting a small delay in exchange for correctness.
questions.deepDive: This connects to a broader principle: optimistic UI is a good tool for state where a brief, self-correcting inconsistency is an acceptable cost (e.g. a like button), but it's the wrong tool where the displayed number is used to make real operational decisions, like whether there's enough stock to fulfill an order.
questions.weak: A weak answer can't name a concrete failure mode and just says "we made sure it was accurate" without explaining how.
followUps: Would you ever use optimistic updates for inventory-adjacent UI, and where would the line be?

questions.question: How did JWT-aware API integration work in Angular specifically?
questions.thirtySec: An HttpInterceptor attached the JWT to outgoing requests and centrally handled 401 responses (redirect to login or refresh), so individual services/components never handled auth headers directly.
questions.ninetySec: Angular's HttpInterceptor let me centralize JWT handling: it attached the Authorization header to every outgoing request and intercepted 401 responses to redirect to login (or attempt a token refresh, depending on what the backend supported), rather than each feature module's service needing to remember to attach the token or handle expiry itself. This also gave one place to add request/response logging or error normalization consistently across all modules.
questions.deepDive: Centralizing this in an interceptor also made it much easier to change auth behavior later — for example, adding refresh-token logic only required changing the interceptor, not every service across six-plus modules.
questions.weak: A weak answer has JWT attachment logic duplicated in each Angular service instead of centralized in an interceptor.
followUps: What did you do if a 401 happened while a background request (not a user-initiated action) was in flight?

questions.question: How were role-based modules controlled in the Angular app?
questions.thirtySec: Route guards checked a role-to-module access map before allowing navigation into a module, and the same map drove which navigation links were shown — with the backend independently enforcing permissions on every request.
questions.ninetySec: I maintained a role → allowed-modules/actions configuration, and Angular route guards checked against it before allowing navigation into a module's routes, redirecting away if the current user's role didn't have access. The same configuration drove the navigation menu, so users never saw links into modules they couldn't access. As with every other project, this was explicitly a UX layer — the backend enforced authorization independently on every API call, regardless of what the frontend chose to show or hide.
questions.deepDive: Keeping this as configuration data (rather than scattered `if role === X` checks in guards and components) meant adding a new role or adjusting an existing role's access was a data change, not a code change across many files.
questions.weak: A weak answer scatters role checks ad hoc across guards and components with no single source of truth, or implies frontend gating alone is sufficient security.
followUps: How would you audit that the role-to-module configuration matched what the backend actually enforced?
questions.honestyWarning: Always state that backend authorization enforcement is required and independent of frontend route guards.
